old: Anyone examining Vedic scholarship will see that Sayanacharya's commentary, faults and all, has not been surpassed. Even its critics must acknowledge its special mastery.
new: Anyone who examines how Vedic study has proceeded must admit that, whatever its faults and omissions, Vedic study would not be possible without Sayanacharya's commentary. Those who have only recently entered this field may decry it as written merely to display scholarship; but those who revile the commentary do not know how helpful it is for first entering this impregnable fortress, nor what a skilled guide Sayanacharya is, nor how much they themselves are indebted to it. Who does not know that a first translation of any work, however faulty, is very useful, and that the faults of the first attempts help later workers and make them follow the right road and leave the by-paths? So if we can now explain better than Sayanacharya, we must not forget that we came this far with his help. Like Max Müller, every student of the Veda who thinks calmly must gratefully remember the service rendered by Sayanacharya.
basis: Kannada p.302: without Sayana the Veda could not be studied; critics do not know how much they owe him; English had "has not been surpassed ... special mastery"

old: This field was not empty before Sayana, nor did he claim to be its first pioneer — as already discussed, earlier commentaries offered real help, but Sayana's own text has one quality theirs lack: ease of understanding without excessive effort. Sayanacharya himself, in composing his commentary, drew on and names many predecessors: Bhattabhaskara, Skandasvami, Atmananda, the Nirukta-authors, Bashkala, Kashyapa, the Aitihasikas (traditional historians), the Naidanas (Nidana-sutra experts), grammarians (Vyakaranikas), tradition-bearers (Sampradaya-vids), self-knowers (Atmavids), elder-teachers (Vriddhashasanas), and earlier commentary-authors such as Devasvami — among others.
new: As already said, Sayanacharya gives several derivations for a single word, and for a single mantra not only his own view but also the views of earlier scholars. Many earlier views and works are cited, but nothing is properly told about them. He mentions Bhattabhaskaramishra, Skandasvami, Kapardisvami and others, and uses the terms Nairukta (the Nirukta authors), Aitihasika (the Puranikas), Shabdika (the grammarians), Sampradayavid (those who knew the tradition), Atmavid (the knowers), Vriddhashasana, Purve bhashyakritah (the earlier commentators) and Apare kechana (some others). So many had worked in this same field by the time Sayanacharya composed his commentary, and it must be said that he composed it on the basis of their works.
basis: Kannada p.302 lists Bhattabhaskaramishra, Skandasvami, Kapardisvami and the terms Nairukta, Aitihasika, Shabdika, Sampradayavid, Atmavid, Vriddhashasana, purve bhashyakritah, apare kechana; English had Atmananda, Bashkala, Kashyapa, Naidanas, Devasvami (not in print) and a claim that his text alone is easy to follow

old: Other lesser-known Rigveda commentaries are also mentioned in passing: the Ravana-bhashya, Kaushika-bhashya, Gaudartha-vritti, and works by scholars in the lineage of Bhavasvami, Sthanaka, and Madhavadeva. None of these approach the completeness of Sayanacharya's own commentary, and none survive to us today.
new: The names of some other Ṛgveda commentaries also occur: the Ravana-bhashya, the Kaushika-bhashya, the Gudhartharatnamala and others. Devaraja, the commentator on the Nirukta, cites in his commentary the Veda-commentaries of Bhavasvami, Rahadeva, Shrinivasa, Madhavadeva and others. All these seem to be earlier than Sayanacharya, but none of their works can now be found.
basis: Kannada p.302: Devaraja cites Bhavasvami, Rahadeva, Shrinivasa, Madhavadeva; English had "Sthanaka", "Gaudartha-vritti", omitted Rahadeva and Shrinivasa

old: Mahidhara's and Uvata's Yajurveda-commentaries, though well-known, offer no help for the Rigveda — only the commentaries already discussed serve that purpose.
new: The Yajurveda commentaries of Mahidhara and Uvata are very famous, but they are not so helpful for the Ṛgveda commentary; only in understanding the ṛks that are common to the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda can the two commentaries be compared.
basis: Kannada p.303: not so helpful for Rgveda, but the two can be compared for ṛks common to both; English said no help at all and added "only the commentaries already discussed"

old: in that early era, texts hadn't gained much traction
new: in that early time language had no script or similar means

old: Study paused on Paurnamasa, Ashtami, Chaturdashi, Purnima, and eclipse days. Each morning, after his own rituals, the guru assigned the day's or week's new lesson in fixed sequence; students practiced the previous lesson before receiving the new one. In this way, students worked through the entire Samhita along with its corresponding Brahmana, Aranyaka, and Upanishads — alongside the Vedangas (Shiksha, etc.), Kalpasutra, Dharmashastra, Puranas, and Itihasa — pausing during the Ashadha rainy season. This full course was reckoned to take roughly **twelve years**.
new: On the days other than the non-study days (Pratipad, Ashtami, Chaturdashi, Purnima, Amavasya and Sankramana), early in the morning, after bath, sandhya, the fire-rite and the other morning duties, the disciple sits humbly near the guru, facing north, and the guru teaches him the lesson daily for a month or more. When the lesson seems enough, the guru begins the next in the same way, and the disciple recites the earlier lesson well every day, as the guru said. While he studies the Veda in this way, at midday and whenever else there is opportunity he also studies the six Vedangas (Shiksha and the rest), the Kalpasutra, Dharmashastra, Puranas and Itihasa and other books. It was decided that to study one Veda completely in this way takes roughly **twelve years**.
basis: Kannada p.303: non-study days are Pratipad, Ashtami, Chaturdashi, Purnima, Amavasya, Sankramana; no Ashadha pause, no Brahmana/Aranyaka/Upanishad; lessons last a month or more; English had Paurnamasa, eclipse days, Ashadha rainy season

new: ...When the study of one's own shakha is complete, if there is time and capacity, the other shakhas (the other Vedas) may also be studied. After the studies are over, the disciple satisfies the guru with a fitting dakshina, performs the snataka-vrata, marries and may become a householder.
basis: Kannada p.304: other shakhas (other Vedas) if time and strength allow; after studies guru-dakshina, snataka-vrata, marriage, grihastha; English omitted vrata and marriage and added "further shastras"

new: ## Chapter Nineteen
basis: Kannada p.309: ಹತ್ತೊಂಭತ್ತನೆಯ ಪ್ರಕರಣ (nineteenth chapter); the heading stands in the English page 308 section

old: Even as some of our own scholars neglected our ancient culture, foreigners embraced these texts, writing extensively in books and articles
new: Their regard for our country's ancient culture is shown by the articles and books they have written after reading our texts
basis: Kannada p.309: no statement that our own scholars neglected the culture

old: Among Western scholars, **German scholars in particular have excelled** — owed to German's own recorded historical-linguistic connection to Sanskrit, a connection no other Western language shares to the same degree.
new: Among Western scholars, **German scholars in particular** have studied the Vedic texts more than any others. The Ṛgveda has not been translated into any language of our country, but there are two translations in German and two in English; notes and articles on the Veda are countless; and there is a Sanskrit dictionary in German written from the historical point of view, such as no other language has.
basis: Kannada p.309: no Ṛgveda translation in any Indian language; two in German, two in English; a historical Sanskrit-German dictionary; English had an invented reason (German linguistic connection to Sanskrit)

old: Western scholars find it natural to critically examine texts this way; our own readers, working from more traditional viewpoints, have found a purely academic approach less immediately comfortable to adopt. It must be acknowledged, though, that Western scholarship has shown one imprudent tendency: treating certain received Vedic traditions as unnecessary to accept at face value — though this isn't every Western scholar's stated position. Since this discipline is comparatively recent, it's unsurprising that not everything in their work is fully correct — but this doesn't diminish its overall value; these texts remain extremely useful for understanding the Vedas.
new: Western authors have one advantage in criticism: our writers cannot easily write or criticise in a way that puts the subject first and leaves aside certain traditional opinions, whereas Westerners can easily give priority to the subject. Their writing has also one disadvantage: to grasp many points in the Vedas, acquaintance with the tradition is essential, and without it the meaning is not understood. Because of this difficulty, everything written in Western books cannot be accepted as correct. For this reason, however, the value of their work should not be thought small; those books are very useful to anyone eager to understand the Veda.
basis: Kannada p.309: tradition-knowledge is essential for the Vedas, so Western books cannot be accepted wholesale; English said Westerners treat traditions as unnecessary and that the discipline is recent

old: In the mid-18th century, the French writer **Voltaire** spoke highly of Brahmins' wisdom, and a text called "Ezour-Vedam" (a spurious "Veda") became known at Oxford in translation. **William Jones** translated Kalidasa's *Shakuntala* into English. **Colebrooke** later wrote an influential essay on the Vedas.
new: In the middle of the eighteenth century the well-known French writer **Voltaire** praised the intellectual power of the Brahmins that is seen in the four Vedas. In 1784 the Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded to study ancient literature. **Wilkins** translated the Bhagavad Gita the next year. In 1805 **Colebrooke** wrote an essay on the subject "The Vedas are the sacred books of the Hindus". It is commendable that he wrote such a valuable essay in the conditions of that time.
basis: Kannada p.310: Voltaire; Asiatic Society of Bengal 1784; Wilkins translated the Gita the next year; Colebrooke 1805; English had Ezour-Vedam and William Jones/Shakuntala (not in print) and no dates

old: Colebrooke's essay deserves special mention for candidly describing the Veda's linguistic difficulty, advising that no one seeking full understanding of the Veda should neglect this challenge. His observations held for a long time, though later, deeper Sanskrit scholarship moved past some of his specific conclusions — even so, his pioneering effort, undertaken before Sanskrit studies had matured, deserves real credit.
new: At the end of the essay he wrote: "The language of the Veda is very difficult. To read and translate the whole Veda is hard; great effort is needed to grasp the profound matters in it; but those who study Oriental literature must look into these books from time to time." These views cannot be called correct. But it is a great wonder that those who earlier disliked Sanskrit and abused those who studied it, once they began the study of the Veda, praised it without reserve and became guides to later students of Sanskrit.
basis: Kannada p.310: Colebrooke's closing words and the remark that these men first disliked Sanskrit; English had "observations held for a long time ... pioneering effort"

old: Following him, the French scholar **Eugène Burnouf** edited and published the Rigveda Samhita from many gathered manuscripts, building on Colebrooke's work — though he could complete only part of it before his death.
new: Twenty years later the German scholar **Rorse** set out to publish the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā on the basis of the palm-leaf manuscripts Colebrooke had collected, but he died before a very small part had been printed.
basis: Kannada p.310: ರೋರ್ಸೆ (a German), twenty years later, from Colebrooke's manuscripts; English had French scholar Burnouf (not in print)

old: The German scholar **Rudolph Roth**, in the *St. Petersburg Sanskrit-German Lexicon* (8 volumes), traced Vedic-era word usage across all its varying senses with example sentences for each — a work whose usefulness Vedic scholars still rely on today.
new: The St. Petersburg Sanskrit-German Lexicon (7 volumes), published under the editorship of the two scholars **Roth** and **Bothling**, shows their devotion and industry. In it, for each word, the changes of meaning from the Vedic period to the present, and all the sentences in which the word occurs, are brought together and explained. No student of the Veda can deny the usefulness of this dictionary.
basis: Kannada p.310: ೭ ಭಾಗಗಳು (7 volumes), edited by Roth and Bothling; English had 8 volumes and "Rudolph Roth" alone

old: grammar, Nirukta, and lexicography comprehensively
new: grammar, word-collections and the like comprehensively

old: The German scholar **Franz Bopp** studied Sanskrit primarily for comparative linguistics rather than Vedic interpretation specifically — his writings are more introductory in nature, focused on language comparison across the broader Indo-European family rather than Sanskrit alone. Even so, his contribution to Sanskrit scholarship generally was substantial...
new: **Max Müller**, a man of great intellect, stands foremost among those who studied the Sanskrit language and wrote books; there is no branch he has not touched. He has written on the interpretation of the Veda, the science of language, history, Vedanta, grammar and every other subject. All his writings are in the form of lectures, and his style is very simple; it has been a great help in making the Sanskrit language and learning popular. More than all this, he did not study Sanskrit as a foreigner; with the same attitude as our own countrymen would have...
basis: Kannada p.310: the paragraph is about Max Müller; Franz Bopp is not in the print on these pages

old: ...whether Bopp's stated neutrality actually held up in practice is a separate question — writers sharing his broad perspective generally accept traditional textual views as authoritative up to a point, but depart from tradition once critical examination begins, giving priority to the subject itself over inherited convention. Truly impartial scholars on Hindu-shastra topics remain genuinely rare.
new: ...he studied as one of us. Because he wrote with that same attitude, he generally presented the opinions of the books according to tradition; but when criticising he did not write like one bound to tradition; he gave priority to the subject. In Hindu shastra no other European scholar has written as impartially as he.
basis: Kannada p.311: the passage on impartiality is about Max Müller, not Bopp

old: This edition became the foundation of modern Vedic study; before it, study proceeded solely through oral instruction.
new: This edition became a firm foundation for the study of the Veda; from then on the study went forward in an orderly way.

new: the relations between the Hindus, Persians, Greeks and Romans

new: **Muir's** *The Original Sanskrit Texts* (5 volumes)
basis: Kannada p.311: ೫ ಭಾಗಗಳುಳ್ಳ

new: **Dr. Haug** published the Aitareya Brahmana; its introduction is very attractive and contains many useful points.
basis: Kannada p.312: ಐತರೇಯಬ್ರಾಹ್ಮಣ

old: **Wilson** produced a complete English translation of the Rigveda (and also translated the Vishnu Purana and wrote *Hindoo Theatre*). His Rigveda translation closely follows Vedic-language meaning, especially in its early volumes — by his own account, he avoided speculative interpretation where meaning was unclear, preferring to follow Sayana's own commentary over divergent Western annotations wherever the two differed. In a place or two his own era's assumptions surface, but this doesn't diminish the work's overall value.
new: The oldest of the translations of the Ṛgveda is **Wilson's**. He also translated the Vishnu Purana and wrote a book called *Hindoo Theatre*. His translation of the Ṛgveda is very old and the first of such attempts. In Wilson's view, no one is as qualified as the Hindus to write the sacred books of the Hindus; however eager European scholars may be, they cannot convey the sense of the original without contradicting it; native commentaries are better than Western notes, and of the native commentaries Sayana's bhashya is the best. Therefore Wilson wrote his translation following Sayanacharya, and it is useful where Sayana's commentary is not clear. On the whole, Wilson's translation has lost some of its authority as new matters have come to light in course of time.
basis: Kannada p.312: Wilson held Hindus best qualified, followed Sayana because native commentary is better; his translation lost authority with time; English said he avoided speculation and "closely follows Vedic-language meaning" and added an unsupported remark about his era

old: **Ludwig** and **Grassmann**, German scholars, each produced independent German translations with markedly different prose approaches from one another — and both differed sharply from Wilson in places, rejecting the idea that the Veda's meaning can be fully recovered through tradition alone, instead pursuing critical/historical determinations that sometimes yield divergent conclusions.
new: The two German translations by **Ludwig** and **Grassmann** deserve attention; the first is in prose and the second in verse. Both hold views entirely opposed to Wilson's: they think that the true meaning of the Veda cannot be known by Hindus bound to tradition. Wherever possible they try to decide matters from the critical or historical point of view, and because of this their conclusions are in many places peculiar.
basis: Kannada p.312: first prose, second verse; both oppose Wilson; English said both prose and "markedly different prose approaches"

old: **Kaegi** wrote in 1880 a critical German-language study of the Rigveda's subject matter (later translated into English) — cited repeatedly throughout the present work.
new: **Kaegi** wrote in 1880, in German, a lecture on the Ṛgveda; though short, it is very well written from the point of view of criticism. It has been translated into English.
basis: Kannada p.312: a short lecture, translated into English; "cited repeatedly throughout the present work" is not in the print

new: Besides the books mentioned above there are countless articles and reviews; these have been printed in the journals of such bodies as the **German Oriental Society, The American Oriental Society,** and **The Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland**.
basis: Kannada p.313: countless articles and reviews printed in these societies' journals; "scholarly rigor" is not in the print

new: the grammars in common use all relate to later Sanskrit, but this grammar attempts to bring Vedic and non-Vedic grammar together; when the forms of a noun are given, the Vedic forms stand with them (e.g., *devāḥ, devāsaḥ; devaiḥ, devebhiḥ*, both forms standing together)

new: **Shrutibodha** is a recent effort; its aim is to translate the Veda into English and the native languages so that ordinary people can understand it. Though it does useful work in its own way, it is not of much use to one who studies the subject scientifically.

old: The Shatapatha Brahmana states: "Prajapati, wishing to create, needed to know the complete range of eternal ritual-forms and materials needed for creation. He then considered these three: the Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda — known to contain everything." All meters, revealed texts (shrutis), life-force, and deities are said to be contained within it. This is eternal, beginningless, and alone called "Sat" (Being) from time without beginning — the Veda encompassing everything, with no question of it deriving from anything prior. This same subject is discussed in the Purusha-sukta...
new: The Shatapatha Brahmana states: "Prajapati desired to know all the moving and unmoving beings and the whole mass of things in the world. Then he saw that all this is contained in the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda and Samaveda, which are called the Trayī. All kinds of metres, praises, breath and deities were in it. It is eternal; it has no destruction; it is also called Sat (that which is). This Veda contains everything; therefore he thought: I myself shall become of the form of this Veda." On this same subject the Purusha-sukta says...
basis: Kannada p.317: Prajapati wished to know all beings and things; saw all contained in the three Vedas; Veda indestructible, called Sat; he would himself become the Veda; English said he needed to know ritual-forms and materials for creation

old: believing in deities corresponding to natural causes, performing rituals out of unreasoned fear, and composing prayers and hymns from whatever satisfaction or feeling moved them, before having faced great hardship. This isn't a conclusion drawn from the mantras' content directly, but from their careful composition and thoughtfulness, it becomes clear their composers were, from early on, actually quite intellectually mature.
new: taking whatever they saw to be gods, beginning to praise the extraordinary workings of nature, knowing nothing yet of the sorrow and hardship of the world, and, glad like children at everything, singing as it appeared to them. This conclusion was not reached by examining the mantras. After meditating more on the mantras it becomes clear that this view is wrong or needs much correction: the Aryans of the Vedic age were neither uncultured nor barbarians, and the mantras themselves show that civilisation was then in a fairly good state.
basis: Kannada p.321 (no "unreasoned fear"; the view was not reached from the mantras; the Aryans were cultured)

old: **Yet another view** holds that the Rigveda is not a systematic philosophical text at all, but simply a collection of the earliest hymns — pointing to war-themed suktas and the stories of Sarama, Bhrigu, and Angiras as evidence. Drawing comparisons to Phoenician civilization and its interactions with Assyria, Babylonia, Egypt, and Greece, this view holds that linguistic evidence connects ancient Aryan civilization to a broader trade network — the Ganges region once connected to the Mediterranean by water routes now lost to history, explaining why European and Hindu regions later grew disconnected. This remains one hypothesis among several.
new: **Another view** holds that the Ṛgveda is not only a book of verse but also history. Some wars are spoken of in the Ṛgveda, and there is a story of Sarama, the Phanis and the Angirases. On this basis some points have been decided: long ago a great war took place between the Aryans and a people called Phoenicians, both of whom had earlier lived in India or near it; in this war the Phoenicians were defeated and had to go to Greece, Rome and other regions. The Phoenicians were the first of the civilised peoples of the world; the civilisation of the ancient countries Assyria, Babylonia, Egypt, Greece and others has its root in the civilisation of these Phoenicians and Aryans. They had first lived in Afghanistan or the western part of India and, for some reason, migrated to the western countries and settled there. At that time there was a strait joining the Red Sea and the Mediterranean, and through it ship-trade with Europe went on; in course of time the strait was closed, and the trade between Europe and the Hindu countries stopped. This seems to be merely a world of conjecture.
basis: Kannada p.321: story of Sarama, Phani, Angiras (English had Bhrigu); war with Phoenicians; Red Sea-Mediterranean strait (English had Ganges-Mediterranean water routes); "mere world of conjecture"

old: The Rigveda's content can be divided several ways: mantras of ordinary/everyday concern, spiritual (adhyatmic) mantras, and practical/ritual mantras. Deity-focused mantras generally aim to please the deities, concerned with sons, progeny, cattle, and similar worldly goods. Spiritual mantras are comparatively few, including cosmological/metaphysical inquiry alongside more worldly questions — genuinely difficult territory, since even certain deity-worship can be understood in either a worldly or spiritual register, and the line between "practical" and "spiritual" mantras isn't always sharp.
new: The Saṃhitā can be divided more clearly into three kinds: mantras concerned with sacrifices and dharma, spiritual mantras, and worldly (vyavaharika) mantras. The religious mantras are in general addressed to the deities, in the form of praise of them, and of prayer for wealth, sons, cattle and similar things. The spiritual mantras are very few; in them are answers to questions such as who am I, whence did I come, what is the first cause of the world. As for the worldly mantras, it is not easy to separate the religious from the worldly, but a worldly mantra may be taken to be one not addressed directly to the deities.
basis: Kannada p.322: three kinds; spiritual mantras answer who am I, whence, first cause; worldly = not directly addressed to deities

new: The last mantra of that sukta shows what place the woman had in the household and how sacred an act marriage was: "In your house (your husband's house) exercise authority over the mother-in-law, father-in-law, brothers-in-law and sisters-in-law", that is, look after the welfare of all. (10-85-46)
basis: Kannada p.322: the wife is told to look after the in-laws; English made it the bride's own wish for authority

old: Genuinely historically-informative suktas, however, are few. Where they exist, they generally serve to illuminate some royal lineage's history, praising a king's generosity or Indra's favor, revealing how far kings honored the deities and giving the historical basis for the Purohita's role — the rishis maintaining their relationship with the deities through devotion and the expectation of generous gifts in return.
new: Next come the suktas that tell history. They are historical only in name; the history to be learned from them is very little. In general these suktas tell of the victory of some kings or royal families and of their praising Indra for the victory. Kings can please the deities only through purohitas; for this they take refuge in great rishis such as Vishvamitra. These rishis, besides satisfying the deities, also sing the praise of the master (the donor).
basis: Kannada p.322

old: Marriage was arranged by the father; widow remarriage appears to have been considered acceptable. Details of husband-wife relations are scarce, but the **wife held a significant position within the household** — "household deity, mistress of the household" — with authority over domestic affairs; there's little evidence of exclusive husbandly authority in this domain. A house without a mistress, it's noted, could not properly function; a newly arrived young bride becomes the household's own yajamana (ritual mistress). This blessing was offered to a bride newly arriving in her husband's home:
new: The father was the master of the house. Marriage was regarded as very sacred; no bond was subtler than that between husband and wife. The wife's place in the house was very high; a house without her was thought to be no house (*gṛhiṇī gṛhamucyate*). In the homa and sacrifices she has equal authority with her husband, and if the husband is away from the place for some reason she has the authority to perform the homa. In her husband's house she herself is the mistress of the house. When she goes to her husband's house for the first time she is blessed with this mantra:
basis: Kannada p.327: father the master; marriage sacred; wife has equal authority in homa; English had "widow remarriage appears acceptable" (contradicts p.328) and "young bride becomes yajamana"
